analysis.one_liner: Allows companies to own a city's newspaper and its radio or TV stations at the same time.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in January 2001, sent to two House subcommittees, and it died without a vote when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since the 1970s, the FCC has barred a company from owning both a daily newspaper and a broadcast station (AM, FM, or TV) in the same market, to keep multiple independent local news sources. This bill ordered the FCC to strike that restriction from its rules within 90 days, so one company could control a town's newspaper and its TV or radio stations together.
analysis.who_benefits: Large media companies and newspaper chains that want to buy or already own broadcast stations in the same markets as their newspapers. Owning both lets one company capture a market's print and broadcast audience together, which is valuable for advertising revenue and for setting the local news agenda.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large newspaper and broadcast media companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the FCC to modify its rules so that ownership of a daily newspaper can no longer be a basis for denying or limiting an AM, FM, or TV broadcast license, including for parties under common control.
The FCC would have to complete all actions needed to make this change within 90 days after the bill's enactment.
The bill would eliminate provisions that limit granting or renewal of broadcast licenses based on a party's ownership, operation, or control of a daily newspaper.

analysis.who_pays: Readers, viewers, and listeners in local markets where one company would come to own both the newspaper and broadcast outlets, reducing the number of independent local news voices. Smaller independent broadcasters and newspapers would also face a larger combined competitor.
analysis.who_pays_short: Local news audiences in consolidated markets

drawbacks.text: The newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership rule exists to preserve a diversity of local news sources; removing it would allow a single company to control a market's daily newspaper plus its TV and radio stations, concentrating local news coverage in fewer hands.

The bill imposes its change by flat congressional directive and a 90-day deadline, removing the FCC's discretion to weigh competition, diversity, and localism concerns case by case before rewriting the rule.

A good-faith argument for the change: as daily newspapers lose advertising revenue to broadcast and online outlets, allowing cross-ownership could give struggling newspapers a stronger combined business, and defenders of the ban's repeal argue ownership limits should not force newspapers to shrink or close. That benefit to newspaper economics would come at the price of fewer independent owners in each local market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain would flow mainly to large media companies through more consolidated markets; the cost would fall on local news diversity, since one company could control a city's paper and its broadcast stations at once. The strongest case for the bill is the financial pressure on newspapers, but the bill does not limit its change to cases where a newspaper is failing, so the consolidation would be broad and permanent.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it down to two subcommittees, and no one ever brought it up for a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Oxley introduced the bill in the House on January 6, 2001, joined by one cosponsor, Rep. Ralph Hall of Texas.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
On February 7, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet.
On June 18, 2001, it was also referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality.
No further action was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, so the bill died without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Local news diversity was preserved for now, since the FCC's cross-ownership restrictions remained in force. Large media companies gained nothing from this bill, though the FCC itself later relaxed the rule on its own in 2003 and 2007 after a statutory review of media ownership rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Local news audiences; big media gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Michael G. Oxley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require the FCC to eliminate newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership restrictions.

for.name: Rep. Ralph Hall
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Rep. W.J. 'Billy' Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was assigned to never scheduled it for consideration; it was passed down to two subcommittees and never returned, so the House never voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members touched the bill, a Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor, so no party bloc ever took a recorded position and the outcome turned on committee inaction rather than a partisan vote.

industries.industry: Newspaper publishers and broadcast station owners
industries.note: The bill would let these companies own a daily newspaper and broadcast stations in the same market, capturing a local market's print and broadcast audience together. The cost of that gain falls on the number of independent local news sources.

industries.industry: Smaller independent broadcasters and local news outlets
industries.note: Cross-owned combinations would enter their markets with a built-in newspaper and broadcast pair, making it harder for independent local outlets to compete for audiences and advertisers.
